title: Which OSHA standards require training records or certifications?
description: Which OSHA standards require training certifications or records, what each must contain and how long to keep them, compared as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: There is no single Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) rule for training records. Individual standards in 29 CFR parts 1910 and 1926 each set their own documentation duty: some require a signed certification with set contents, such as lockout/tagout, powered industrial trucks and permit-required confined spaces; some set a retention period, such as bloodborne pathogens (3 years) and asbestos (1 year after employment ends); and many, including PPE and 1910.269, require no record at all.
keyTakeaways: Documentation duties are standard by standard. Certification contents, signatures and retention all vary, so a single template rarely fits every standard.
Only a few standards set a retention period for training records: bloodborne pathogens (3 years from training), asbestos (1 year beyond employment), and PSDI press operators (duration of employment).
Several certifications require only the latest record to be kept, such as construction fall protection under 1926.503(b)(2) and logging under 1910.266(i)(10)(ii).
The current text of the PPE standard, 1910.132, has no training certification paragraph; its only certification is the hazard assessment under (d)(2).
Where no record is required, the duty to train still applies, and the employer carries the burden of showing it was met.
jurisdiction: United States (federal, with state plan variations)
regulator: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), US Department of Labor
appliesTo: General industry and construction employers subject to OSHA standards with training provisions
Safety, training and HR teams that design training records and retention schedules
Auditors and compliance teams preparing for OSHA inspections

sections.heading: Is there one OSHA rule for training records?

blocks.text: No. Training documentation is set inside each standard that requires training, and the wording differs. OSHA's own compilation, [Training Requirements in OSHA Standards](https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/osha2254.pdf) (OSHA 2254, 2015 edition), reproduces each training provision standard by standard for this reason. It also notes that it is guidance and creates no new legal obligations, and some of its entries reproduce wording that has since been revised, so the current eCFR text is the authority.

Three patterns appear across the standards. Some require a **certification**: a signed or dated statement by the employer that named employees were trained. Some require a **training record** with listed contents and a retention period. Many require **no record**, leaving the employer to decide how to show compliance. The table below compares the main examples.

sections.heading: How do certifications differ from training records?

blocks.text: A certification is a statement that the training duty was met; a training record describes the training itself. The lockout/tagout certification needs only names and dates. The bloodborne pathogens record needs the content or a summary and the qualifications of the trainer, which lets an inspector judge whether the training was adequate, not just whether it happened.

Signature requirements also vary. Permit-required confined spaces call for the signatures or initials of the trainers. Construction fall protection, logging and PSDI press training accept the signature of the trainer or the employer. Lockout/tagout and powered industrial trucks do not mention a signature, although the truck certification must identify the person who trained or evaluated the operator. Two certifications also cover prior training: where the employer relies on training given by another employer (1926.503(b)(1)) or before the employee was hired (1910.266(i)(10)(i)), or completed before the standard took effect, the record must show the date the employer determined that the prior training was adequate.

blocks.title: Watch for outdated guidance
blocks.text: Some widely copied checklists cite a PPE training certification under 1910.132(f)(4). The current text published on osha.gov and in the eCFR contains only paragraphs (f)(1) to (f)(3). Likewise, the 2015 OSHA 2254 compilation reproduces an earlier 1910.269 certification that the current text replaces with a non-mandatory note. Build record templates from the current regulation text.

sections.heading: What should employers keep when a standard requires no record?

blocks.text: Keep enough to prove the training duty was met, because the duty to train does not depend on a record. Standards without a prescribed record still set conditions an inspector will test: that hearing conservation training happened annually (1910.95(k)(2)), that PPE users demonstrated understanding and ability before working (1910.132(f)(2)), and that power workers demonstrated proficiency before training was considered complete (1910.269(a)(2)(viii)).

A practical minimum, mirroring the most detailed prescribed record (bloodborne pathogens), is: employee name and job title, date, content version or summary, trainer and qualifications, and the method used to verify understanding. Process safety management already requires the last element, and it is what separates evidence of competence from evidence of attendance. Related standards pages show how this applies in practice: [OSHA lockout/tagout](/regulations/osha-lockout-tagout-training-requirements), [OSHA forklift operator training](/regulations/osha-forklift-operator-training-requirements), [OSHA bloodborne pathogens](/regulations/osha-bloodborne-pathogens-training-requirements) and [OSHA PPE training](/regulations/osha-personal-protective-equipment-training).

sections.heading: How should employers set retention periods for OSHA training records?

blocks.text: Apply the stated period where one exists and set a documented period where none does. Retention clocks start at different events: the date of training for bloodborne pathogens, separation from employment for asbestos, and the end of employment for PSDI press operators. Certifications kept as "latest" or "most recent" are superseded rather than expired, so the system must retain the current one for as long as the employee remains in the role.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry stores each standard's documentation rule as part of its framework: the required fields, who signs, and the retention trigger. A single training event can then produce the certification or record each applicable standard requires, with the verification method recorded alongside it.

faqs.q: How long must OSHA training records be kept?
faqs.a: It depends on the standard. Bloodborne pathogens records are kept 3 years from training, asbestos records 1 year beyond the last date of employment, and PSDI press certifications for the duration of employment. Lockout/tagout, forklift and PSM training documentation have no stated period.

faqs.q: Does OSHA accept electronic training records and signatures?
faqs.a: The standards compared here specify contents, not format, except where a signature or initials are named. Employers using electronic records should make sure the required fields are captured and that signatures, where required, are attributable to the named trainer or employer.

Section 1910.178 does not set an expiry for the certification. It requires a performance evaluation at least once every three years under (l)(4)(iii), and the certification must include the evaluation date, so in practice the record is updated at least every three years.

faqs.q: Can employees see their own training records?
faqs.a: Some standards say so expressly. Bloodborne pathogens training records must be provided on request to employees and their representatives under 1910.1030(h)(3)(ii), and confined space certifications must be available for inspection by employees and their representatives under 1910.146(g)(4).
